vc-x1 0.85.15+de2e9af70fa9

Point one existing local bookmark at one commit, `jj bookmark set
<bookmark> -r <target>`, the repositioning a bookmark needs before
it is pushed, since push only sets the line's bookmark to @-.
Nothing is pushed.

--bookmark names a bookmark that must exist, none being created, and
--target a revset of exactly one commit, a bookmark or a rev. A move
backward or sideways is refused unless --allow-backwards, as jj
refuses it, and a bookmark already at the target is left alone.

-s is required: `w` the work repo, `a` the agent repo or `b` both with
--yes, the same name in each and the target resolved in each, every
repo checked before any moves. `p` takes the repo from -R, required,
as it is, with no workspace checks, so careful use is yours.

Usage: vc-x1 move-bookmark [OPTIONS] --bookmark <NAME> --target <REV> --scope <SCOPE>

Options:
      --bookmark <NAME>
          The bookmark to move, which must already exist

  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

      --target <REV>
          Where it moves to, a revset of exactly one commit, a bookmark or a
          rev, resolved in each repo of the scope

      --allow-backwards
          Move it backward or sideways, as `jj` allows it

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

  -R, --repo <PATH>
          Where: a path in the workspace for `-s w|a|b`, or the repo itself for
          `-s p`, required there [default: the current directory]

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

  -s, --scope <SCOPE>
          Which repos, required: `w|work`, `a|agent`, `b|both`, or `p|por`, `a`
          and `b` with --yes, `p` with -R
          
          [possible values: work, agent, both, por]

  -y, --yes
          Move a bookmark in the agent repo, `-s a` or `-s b`

      --dry-run
          Dry run: show what would be done without executing

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

### feat: push refuses a bookmark move that is not forward

Picked from `## Todo` as **push refuses rewriting the work trunk** (wink + agent, 2026-10-28), filed
in the discussion of **squash takes paths**, which became **squash takes --include**, and widened at
its opening's review from the trunk to every bookmark (wink, 2026-10-28). Run in the v0.3.1 form,
wink's call (2026-10-28): every cycle from now on.

#### Problem

`squash` refuses folding into a commit on the trunk's remote without `--yes`, but a squash is local,
and a rewrite reaches anyone else only when it is pushed. There nothing refuses it: push moves a
bookmark backward or sideways when its remote has not moved since the fetch, so a rewritten commit
replaces the published one without a word, on any bookmark. The guard is on the command that cannot
do the harm, missing from the one that can, and it holds the `--yes` that **squash takes --include**
needs for its approval. The trunk the guard names is `[cycle] trunk`, else a hard-coded `main`, a
name no more special than `master`. Push's help also says it publishes "a rung's pair", which only
`-s b` does.

#### Solution

- push refuses a bookmark move that is not forward unless `--rewrite` is given: forward is the
  remote's commit an ancestor of the new one, and anything else, backward or sideways, is a
  rewrite. The refusal names the bookmark, the commit on the remote, the one it would move to, and
  `--rewrite`. A new bookmark and a fast-forward push as before.
  - Every bookmark alike, no name special, in every scope: the work half, the agent half, `-r`'s
    name alone, and `-s p`'s plain repo.
  - The agent half's `main` moves forward in a rung's push, its partner just committed, so it needs
    nothing. A re-fold into a published partner is sideways and takes `--rewrite` like any other.
  - `commit` passes `--rewrite` through to the push it makes, and Land and `commit --closing` move
    forward, a fast-forward or a merge onto the trunk.
  - `squash-push` is the rewrite of published history by purpose, its prompt its approval, as the
    user's `squash-push -s a` folds the session tail into the agent `main` every time.
- squash warns rather than refuses: a fold into a published commit goes ahead, and its rewrite
  warning names `push --rewrite` as what publishes it. squash's `--yes` retires as `--dev` did,
  hidden and refused, naming `push --rewrite`.
- The trunk a closing merges onto and `--land` lands on is `--land`'s bookmark, else the remote's
  default branch, `origin`'s `HEAD`, and a repo with none recorded is refused naming `--land
  <TRUNK>`. `[cycle] trunk` retires, `validate-config` reporting it with its replacement.
- Push's help and module doc say what each scope publishes, the pair only for `-s b`, and the
  README and the agent-files follow.

#### Acceptance check

`cargo test` passes with tests that:

- push `-s w`, `-s a`, and `-s p` refuse a bookmark whose new commit does not descend from its
  remote, backward and sideways, naming `--rewrite`, and push it with the flag
- a new bookmark, a fast-forward, and a rung's agent `main` push as before, and `commit` passes
  `--rewrite` through
- squash folds into a published commit with a warning naming `push --rewrite`, and `squash --yes`
  is refused naming what replaced it
- a closing with no `--land` merges onto the remote's default branch, one with no default recorded
  is refused naming `--land`, and `validate-config` reports `[cycle] trunk`.

#### Deliberation

- The trunk is not special, wink's call (2026-10-28): `main` is only git's and GitHub's default
  name, `master` the old one. What matters is the move, so the rule is every bookmark's, not the
  trunk's.
- A squash is local and can be undone, so its guard was on the wrong command. The rewrite reaches
  others at the push, so the guard is there.
- The guard first, then **undo takes back the last operation**, then **squash takes --include**,
  wink's order (2026-10-28): nothing is unguarded between, `--yes` is freed a release before it
  returns with a new meaning, and undo is there for testing squash.
- The agent-repo needs no exemption, wink's point (2026-10-28): its `main` moves forward in a rung's
  push. The agent's first plan exempted it, from squash-push's routine rewrite, which is squash-push's
  own and not push's.
- `--rewrite`, not `--yes`: push's `-y` passes its `--step` gates, and Land calls push with it, so
  one flag must never approve both. `move-bookmark` refuses the same local move unless
  `--allow-backwards`, so the two names are to be aligned, open.
- The trunk is the remote's default branch, (b) of three, wink's call (2026-10-28): a configured key
  alone left an unconfigured repo unguarded, and a hard-coded `main` was the name this cycle stops
  treating as special. With the guard on every bookmark, the trunk is only what a closing lands on,
  so the key goes.
- `push --from <BM|REV> --to <BM|REV>`, wink's idea (2026-10-28), is its own entry, **push --from
  --to moves a bookmark and publishes it**, close to `move-bookmark` and a push in one.
- Multi-step: the push rule, squash's retirement, the trunk, and the help, each reviewable alone.

#### Ladder

- [feat: push refuses a bookmark move that is not forward opening][p0] (current)
- [feat: push refuses a non-forward move without --rewrite][p1]
- [feat: squash warns rather than refuses a published fold][p2]
- [feat: the trunk is --land's or the remote's default branch][p3]
- [docs: push's help says what each scope publishes][p4]
- [feat: push refuses a bookmark move that is not forward closing][p5]

##### feat: push refuses a bookmark move that is not forward opening

Opens the cycle: the Todo moved here and widened to every bookmark, the version bumped.

##### feat: push refuses a non-forward move without --rewrite

Push checks every bookmark it moves, in each scope, and `commit` passes `--rewrite` through.

##### feat: squash warns rather than refuses a published fold

squash's trunk refusal becomes a warning naming `push --rewrite`, and its `--yes` retires.

##### feat: the trunk is --land's or the remote's default branch

`commit --closing` and `--land` read the trunk from `--land` or `origin`'s `HEAD`, and `[cycle]
trunk` retires.

##### docs: push's help says what each scope publishes

Push's help and module doc, the README, and the agent-files.

##### feat: push refuses a bookmark move that is not forward closing

Closing out the cycle.

content.text:
Your two forms are cleaner than today's rule. Here's how they line up with the code, and what they settle:

**1. `vc-x1 push`** is the same as today: the single nearest bookmark at or below `@-`, moved to `@-` and pushed. None is an error. Several is an error that lists them.

**2. `vc-x1 push --bookmark <NAME>`** changes in two ways:
- **A name that doesn't exist becomes an error.** Today a new name is created at `@-` and pushed.
- **NAME no longer has to be on `@-`'s line.** Today an existing NAME must be one of the nearest bookmarks below `@-`. Under your rule, moving NAME to `@-` is forward if NAME's commit is an ancestor of `@-`, and a rewrite otherwise, so it needs `--rewrite`. The forward check replaces the "nearest" restriction, so the two rules become one.

**3. "That bookmark's remote" is new.** Today `git_push_bookmark` hard-codes `origin`. In jj, a local bookmark tracks remote bookmarks by remote (`NAME@origin`, `NAME@upstream`), so:
- **Tracks exactly one remote:** push there.
- **Tracks none:** error, as you said.
- **Tracks several:** error that names them. Rare, but possible with a fork's `origin` and `upstream`.

**4. I'd use `--remote <NAME>` rather than `--to <URL>`.** jj-lib's `push_refs` takes a configured remote's name, not a URL, and jj's own `git push --remote` works the same way. A push to a bare URL leaves no remote-tracking bookmark behind, so the next push would again have "no remote associated", and the forward check would have nothing to compare against. `--remote <NAME>` covers both failing cases:
- **A bookmark with no remote:** push to that configured remote and start tracking it. That's the first push of any new bookmark.
- **A bookmark that tracks several:** pick one.

Adding a remote for a URL is its own act. `init` and `clone` set up `origin` today, and our rules say a remote URL change needs your go. So the error for "no remote" would name `--remote <NAME>`, and list the configured remotes.

**5. Who creates bookmarks then?** `commit --opening` creates the cycle's bookmark and pushes it. That's the main creation path, and it already works. Under this rule it would push to the repo's only configured remote, or need `--remote` when there are several.

Two questions:
- **`-r REV`:** your forms say `@-`. Should `-r` stay as "push REV instead of `@-`", under the same rules, or go?
- **This cycle or not:** it's push's bookmark rule, and it pairs naturally with `--rewrite`. I'd make it part of the first rung, retitled something like **feat: push moves its bookmark forward to its tracked remote**. It also covers much of the **push --from --to** Todo, which I'd then trim. Do you agree?

The plain version: plain push moves the line's bookmark, `--bookmark` names one that must already exist, and either way the push goes to the remote that bookmark tracks, with an error if there's none. Instead of a URL, I'd add `--remote <NAME>` to choose a configured remote, because jj can only track a bookmark against a named remote.

input.description: Read jj git push's full help

content.content:
Push to a Git remote

By default, pushes tracking bookmarks and tags pointing to `remote_bookmarks(remote=<remote>)..@`.
The default can be configured via `revsets.git-push`. Use `--bookmark`/`--tag` to push specific
bookmarks or tags. Use `--all` to push all bookmarks and tags. Use `--change` to generate bookmark
names based on the change IDs of specific commits.

When pushing a bookmark or tag, the command pushes all commits in the range from the remote's
current position up to and including its target commit. Any descendant commits beyond the reference
are not pushed.

If the local reference has changed from the last fetch, push will update the remote reference to the
new position after passing safety checks. This is similar to `git push --force-with-lease` - the
remote is updated only if its current state matches what Jujutsu last fetched.

Unlike in Git, the remote to push to is not derived from the tracked remote bookmarks. Use
`--remote` to select the remote Git repository by name. There is no option to push to multiple
remotes.

Before the command actually moves, creates, or deletes a remote bookmark, it makes several [safety
checks]. If there is a problem, you may need to run `jj git fetch --remote <remote name>` and/or
resolve some [bookmark conflicts].

[safety checks]: https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/bookmarks/#pushing-bookmarks-safety-checks

[bookmark conflicts]: https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/bookmarks/#conflicts

Usage: jj git push [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --remote <REMOTE>
          The remote(s) to push to (can be repeated)
          
          This defaults to the `git.push` setting. If that is not configured, and if there are
          multiple remotes, the remote named "origin" will be used.
          
          By default, the specified pattern matches remote names with glob syntax, e.g., `--remote
          '*'`. You can also use other [string pattern syntax].
          
          [string pattern syntax]: https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/revsets/#string-patterns

  -b, --bookmark <BOOKMARK>
          Push only this bookmark, or bookmarks matching a pattern (can be repeated)
          
          If a bookmark isn't tracking anything yet, the remote bookmark will be tracked
          automatically.
          
          By default, the specified pattern matches bookmark names with glob syntax. You can also
          use other [string pattern syntax].
          
          [string pattern syntax]: https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/revsets/#string-patterns

  -t, --tag <TAG>
          Push only this tag, or tags matching a pattern (can be repeated)
          
          If a tag isn't tracking anything yet, the remote tag will be tracked automatically.
          
          By default, the specified pattern matches tag names with glob syntax. You can also use
          other [string pattern syntax].
          
          [string pattern syntax]: https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/revsets/#string-patterns

      --all
          Push all bookmarks and tags (including new ones)

      --tracked
          Push all tracked bookmarks and tags
          
          This usually means that the bookmark or tag was already pushed to or fetched from the
          [relevant remote].
          
          [relevant remote]: https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/bookmarks#remotes-and-tracked-bookmarks

      --deleted
          Push all deleted bookmarks and tags
          
          Only tracked bookmarks and tags can be successfully deleted on the remote. A warning will
          be printed if any untracked bookmarks or tags on the remote correspond to missing local
          bookmarks or tags.

      --allow-empty-description
          Allow pushing commits with empty descriptions

      --allow-private
          Allow pushing commits that are private
          
          The set of private commits can be configured by the `git.private-commits` setting. The
          default is `none()`, meaning all commits are eligible to be pushed.

      --allow-conflicts
          Allow pushing commits that contain conflicts

  -r, --revision <REVSETS>
          Push bookmarks and tags pointing to these commits (can be repeated)

  -c, --change <REVSETS>
          Push this commit by creating a bookmark (can be repeated)
          
          The created bookmark will be tracked automatically. Use the `templates.git_push_bookmark`
          setting to customize the generated bookmark name. The default is `"push-" ++
          change_id.short()`.

      --named <NAME=REVISION>
          Specify a new bookmark name and a revision to push under that name, e.g. '--named
          myfeature=@'
          
          Automatically tracks the bookmark if it is new.

      --dry-run
          Only display what will change on the remote

  -o, --option <OPTION>
          Git push options

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

Global Options:
  -R, --repository <REPOSITORY>
          Path to repository to operate on
          
          By default, Jujutsu searches for the closest .jj/ directory in an ancestor of the current
          working directory.

      --ignore-working-copy
          Don't snapshot the working copy, and don't update it
          
          By default, Jujutsu snapshots the working copy at the beginning of every command. The
          working copy is also updated at the end of the command, if the command modified the
          working-copy commit (`@`). If you want to avoid snapshotting the working copy and instead
          see a possibly stale working-copy commit, you can use `--ignore-working-copy`. This may be
          useful e.g. in a command prompt, especially if you have another process that commits the
          working copy.
          
          Loading the repository at a specific operation with `--at-operation` implies
          `--ignore-working-copy`.

      --no-integrate-operation
          Run the command as usual but don't integrate any operations
          
          When this option is given, the operations will still be created as usual but they will not
          be integrated to the operation log. The working copy will also not be updated.
          
          The command will print the resulting operation ID. You can pass that to e.g. `jj --at-op`
          to inspect the resulting repo state, or you can pass it to `jj op restore` to restore the
          repo to that state. You can also pass the ID to `jj op integrate` to integrate the
          operation.
          
          Note that this does *not* prevent side effects outside the repo. For example, `jj git push
          --no-integrate-operation` will still perform the push.

      --ignore-immutable
          Allow rewriting immutable commits
          
          By default, Jujutsu prevents rewriting commits in the configured set of immutable commits.
          This option disables that check and lets you rewrite any commit but the root commit.
          
          This option only affects the check. It does not affect the `immutable_heads()` revset or
          the `immutable` template keyword.

      --at-operation <AT_OPERATION>
          Operation to load the repo at
          
          Operation to load the repo at. By default, Jujutsu loads the repo at the most recent
          operation, or at the merge of the divergent operations if any.
          
          You can use `--at-op=<operation ID>` to see what the repo looked like at an earlier
          operation. For example `jj --at-op=<operation ID> st` will show you what `jj st` would
          have shown you when the given operation had just finished. `--at-op=@` is pretty much the
          same as the default except that divergent operations will never be merged.
          
          Use `jj op log` to find the operation ID you want. Any unambiguous prefix of the operation
          ID is enough.
          
          When loading the repo at an earlier operation, the working copy will be ignored, as if
          `--ignore-working-copy` had been specified.
          
          It is possible to run mutating commands when loading the repo at an earlier operation.
          Doing that is equivalent to having run concurrent commands starting at the earlier
          operation. There's rarely a reason to do that, but it is possible.
          
          [alias: --at-op]

      --debug
          Enable debug logging

      --color <WHEN>
          When to colorize output
          
          [possible values: always, never, debug, auto]

      --quiet
          Silence non-primary command output
          
          For example, `jj file list` will still list files, but it won't tell you if the working
          copy was snapshotted or if descendants were rebased.
          
          Warnings and errors will still be printed.

      --no-pager
          Disable the pager

      --config <NAME=VALUE>
          Additional configuration options (can be repeated)
          
          The name should be specified as TOML dotted keys. The value should be specified as a TOML
          expression. If string value isn't enclosed by any TOML constructs (such as array
          notation), quotes can be omitted.

      --config-file <PATH>
          Additional configuration files (can be repeated)

continue reading, I fixed a typo

I read it through. Three things stand out, and one of them cuts against this cycle's direction:

**1. jj doesn't take the remote from the bookmark.** In its own words: "Unlike in Git, the remote to push to is not derived from the tracked remote bookmarks." The remote is `--remote <NAME>`, else the `git.push` setting, else `origin`, else the only remote. So the "that bookmark's remote" I sketched is git's behavior, not jj's. A URL isn't supported either, only remote names.

**2. jj doesn't move bookmarks when it pushes.** `jj git push` pushes bookmarks where they already point:
- `--bookmark` pushes that bookmark, tracking it automatically if it's new.
- `-r` pushes the bookmarks pointing at those commits.
- `--named NAME=REV` creates a new bookmark at REV and pushes it.

Moving the line's bookmark up to `@-` is a separate step in jj. vc-x1's push does both at once. That's a deliberate addition, and it goes with the pair: the rung's commit always lands at `@-`.

**3. jj doesn't refuse a rewrite at push. It refuses it at the rewrite.** Its push safety check is force-with-lease: the remote moves only if it's still where jj last fetched it. Backward and sideways moves go through. What jj refuses is rewriting immutable commits, with `--ignore-immutable` to override. By default the immutable set is `trunk()`, tags, and untracked remote bookmarks. So jj's model is the one squash had: the guard sits at the local rewrite, and the trunk is special, `trunk()` being the remote's default branch. That's the opposite of what this cycle set out to do.

So "what jj does" offers two consistent models:

- **(A) Follow jj.** The trunk is immutable, and squash, describe, and anything that rewrites it is refused locally without an override. Push is force-with-lease and refuses nothing else. Pushed topic bookmarks rewrite freely, as jj intends. This cycle would shrink to: squash's guard stays and is renamed to jj's terms (`--ignore-immutable`, defined by `trunk()`), plus push's help fix, plus `--remote` and `--named` with jj's meanings.
- **(B) This cycle's rule.** Any non-forward push needs `--rewrite`, and no bookmark is special. It's stricter than jj on every topic bookmark: each review fix folded into a pushed draft needs `--rewrite`. And it puts the guard where jj doesn't.

Either way, push's flags should be a proper subset of jj's, with the same names and meanings: `--remote` (with jj's default rule), `-b/--bookmark`, `-r`, `--named`, `--dry-run`. vc-x1 adds only what the model needs: scope and the pair, the trailers, and moving the line's bookmark to `@-`. `--to <URL>` and "the bookmark's own remote" go, and `--remote` covers both.

My recommendation is (A). Its rule is "published history others build on is protected where you'd change it, and the rest moves freely", which matches how jj users already think, with `trunk()` defined as (b) already says. It does mean accepting that the trunk is special. Not by name, but as `trunk()`, the remote's default branch.

The plain version: jj pushes bookmarks where they already are, to a remote you choose by name, and allows rewrites at push. Its protection is that the trunk's commits can't be changed locally without an override. We can copy that model and make push's flags match jj's, or keep this cycle's stricter "every push must move forward" rule, which jj doesn't have.

Which model, (A) or (B)?

revset-aliases."trunk()" = '''
latest(
  remote_bookmarks(exact:"main", exact:"origin") |
  remote_bookmarks(exact:"master", exact:"origin") |
  remote_bookmarks(exact:"trunk", exact:"origin") |
  remote_bookmarks(exact:"main", exact:"upstream") |
  remote_bookmarks(exact:"master", exact:"upstream") |
  remote_bookmarks(exact:"trunk", exact:"upstream") |
  root()
)
'''
revset-aliases."builtin_log()" = 'present(@) | ancestors(immutable_heads().., 2) | trunk()'
revset-aliases."builtin_immutable_heads()" = '''
trunk() | tags() | untracked_remote_bookmarks() | untracked_remote_tags()

content.text:
The check settles it: in the agent-repo, jj's `trunk()` is `main@origin`, and `immutable_heads()` resolves to the agent `main` tip, `zoxkossq`. So the commit that `squash-push -s a` folds the session tail into is exactly the one jj calls immutable. Raw `jj squash` would refuse it today. vc-x1 only gets away with it because it calls jj-lib directly, below jj's CLI check.

**What (A) does to `squash-push -s a`, applied with no exception:** every run is refused. The agent `main` is that repo's trunk, so its tip is immutable, and the tail can never be folded in. The agent `@` would never be clean.

**Three ways to keep the agent-repo clean:**

1. **squash-push overrides immutability by design**, as jj's `--ignore-immutable` built in. It already asks first when asking is on. `squash-push -s a` behaves exactly as today. The cost: it can fold into any published agent commit, not just the tip, though in practice it only folds into `@-`.
2. **The agent-repo's immutable set is everything but `main`'s tip.** Every older agent commit stays protected, and those are the ones `ochid:` trailers point at, so rewriting them would break the links. The tip is the one commit the session tail folds into. `squash-push -s a` behaves exactly as today, and the exception is as narrow as it can be. jj expresses this as the agent-repo overriding `immutable_heads()`, e.g. `trunk()-`, in the agent-repo's own config. vc-x1 would set that at `init` and read it like jj does.
3. **Never rewrite.** `squash-push -s a` commits the tail as a new forward commit instead of folding it. (A) applies with no exception, but the agent `main` gains a commit per squash-push, and a rung's agent commit no longer holds that rung's whole session. lookup and the `ochid:` pairing were built around one agent commit per rung.

I recommend **2**: it keeps your long-standing `squash-push -s a` unchanged, it protects everything a trailer names, and the exception is written in jj's own terms, so a raw `jj` in the agent-repo agrees with vc-x1.

**Following jj also changes one earlier decision.** jj's `trunk()` isn't the remote's default branch. It's the latest of `main`, `master`, or `trunk` on `origin` or `upstream`, overridable per repo, and `jj git clone` often writes that override for the actual default branch. That fits your point that `master` counts as much as `main`. So I'd use jj's `trunk()` as jj resolves it, reading the user's and repo's alias override, with jj's list as the fallback. That would replace (b) and `[cycle] trunk` alike, and Land and `--closing` would use it too.

**With 2, the reshaped ladder:**

1. **the opening**, retitled to something like **feat: vc-x1 follows jj's immutable commits and push**
2. **immutability:** vc-x1 computes jj's `immutable()` from `trunk()` and `immutable_heads()`, user and repo overrides included. squash and `commit -r` refuse an immutable commit unless `--ignore-immutable`, which replaces squash's `--yes`, and the agent-repo's override lets its tip fold
3. **push:** a subset of jj's flags with jj's meanings: `--remote` with jj's default rule, `-b/--bookmark`, `-r`, `--named`, and `--dry-run`, force-with-lease, plus vc-x1's additions: scope and the pair, the trailers, and moving the line's bookmark to `@-`
4. **trunk:** `--closing` and `--land` use `trunk()`, and `[cycle] trunk` retires
5. **help and docs:** push's help says what each scope publishes, and the README and agent-files follow
6. **the closing**

The plain version: jj treats the agent-repo's latest published commit as untouchable, and that's exactly where `squash-push -s a` folds the session tail. I'd tell vc-x1, the way jj lets a repo be configured, that in the agent-repo only the newest commit stays foldable, so your `squash-push -s a` keeps working unchanged and everything older stays protected.

content.text:
You're not stuck. Most of the way back exists today. The rollback of the push is the missing piece.

## The SHIT scenario

**Locally, nothing is lost.** jj never deletes anything on a rewrite.
- The snapshot of your working copy, with the hours of work, is an operation in `jj op log`. So is the squash, and so is the push's bookmark move.
- The pre-squash `@-` and the `@` that held your work still exist as hidden commits.
- `jj op restore <the op before the squash>` brings it all back: the work uncommitted in `@` again, `@-` as it was, the bookmark where it was.
- vc-x1 already relies on this: squash and push take `jj op` snapshots and restore from them when a stage fails. An `undo` command just exposes that.

**The push is the tricky part, as you said.** The remote now has the bookmark at N, the bad commit, where it used to be at O. Rolling back means pushing the bookmark from N back to O, a backward move. There's a trap:
- A plain `jj op restore` also rewinds jj's record of where the remote is, so jj believes the remote is at O.
- The force-with-lease check then sees the remote really at N, refuses, and reports that the remote changed since the last fetch.
- I believe jj's `op restore` and `undo` take a `--what` option for exactly this: restore the local repo but keep the remote-tracking state, then push. vc-x1's undo would do the same in one step.

**What can't be rolled back:**
- Anyone who fetched N in between still has it. For the agent-repo and a single-user work-repo, that's nobody.
- If the hours of work held a secret, pushing back to O doesn't unpublish it. GitHub keeps unreachable commits fetchable by SHA for a while.

## What that suggests for our rules

The scenario points at a different failure than the one this cycle has been guarding. The danger wasn't "a bookmark moved sideways". It was a command taking far more than you meant, then publishing it, with no chance to see it first. So:

1. **Every local action can be undone, so local actions don't need refusals.** `vc-x1 undo -s w|a|b|p` undoes the last vc-x1 operation in the scoped repos. That requires each vc-x1 write to record, per repo, the operation before it and any remote bookmark moves it made, since the agent-repo's op log moves on its own with every session write. No immutable set and no `--ignore-immutable`. A squash into a published commit still gets the existing warning.
2. **An undo also undoes the push.** If the undone operation published, undo shows what it will push back, `bookmark@origin N → O`, and asks. That's an outward action, so it needs your approval like any push.
3. **A command shows what it takes when that's more than the routine.** This would have prevented the scenario.
   - `squash-push -s b` at rest expects an empty work `@`. A non-empty one gets the file list with `+n -m` and a prompt, the same approval as `squash --include`.
   - `squash-push.yes = true` today skips every prompt, so it would skip only the routine case: the agent tail, or an empty work side.
4. **Pushes use force-with-lease and nothing more.** Backward and sideways moves are allowed, because undo can reverse them, and the lease stops you overwriting a remote someone else moved. In a shared repo, protection for the bookmark others build on is the server's job: GitHub's branch protection refuses force pushes to `main` server-side, for every client, not just vc-x1. So no bookmark is special to vc-x1, which is what you wanted.
5. **The agent-repo stays clean with one command**, `squash-push -s a`, folding the tail into its published tip. Under these rules that's a local rewrite plus a leased push, with no exception needed.

Compared with the current cycle, this replaces "refuse non-forward pushes" with "show what you take, and make everything undoable". The cycle would become:
- squash's `--yes` retires, with squash only warning
- squash-push asks about a non-routine fold, with the file list
- push's help fix
- push's flags made to match jj's where they overlap: `--remote`, `--named`

Undo would be the next cycle, as already ordered. Or it could come first, since it's the actual safety net here.

The plain version: if you squash hours of work by mistake, nothing is truly lost, because jj keeps every earlier state. What's missing is one vc-x1 command that restores it and also pushes the remote bookmark back. Given that, the rules should stop refusing rewrites. Instead, vc-x1 should show you when a command is about to take more than usual, let pushes overwrite only what you last saw, and leave protecting a shared `main` to the server.

content.text:
Yes, undo first, and yes, multi-step. It's the safety net the rule changes lean on, so it should exist before they land. The current opening isn't pushed yet, so this cycle can become the undo cycle at no cost. The push-and-squash rules go back into the Todo, reshaped as last discussed, as the cycle after.

## Design points

**1. Record each run in the op log itself.** Every jj operation carries metadata, and I think jj-lib lets a transaction set tags on its operation. If every vc-x1 write tags its operations with a run id and the command name, then:
- the last run is the newest tagged operation in each repo, and the state before it is the parent of that run's first operation
- what it pushed can be derived by comparing the remote-tracking bookmarks before and after the run

No state file, nothing that can disagree with the repo. I need to confirm the tag API in code.

**2. Restore commits and bookmarks, not the files on disk.** This is the subtle one. A plain `jj op restore` also checks out the old `@`, which rewrites files on disk:
- **The agent-repo:** Claude Code keeps appending to the session's journal file, so a restore would cut it back to its old contents, and the session would keep writing onto the shortened file. Transcript lost.
- **The work-repo:** edits made since the run would be overwritten.

So undo restores the commit graph and bookmarks, then makes `@` hold what's on disk now. In your scenario that's exactly right: the squash didn't touch the files, so after the undo `@-` is the original commit and `@` holds the hours of work again.

**3. Rolling back the push asks first.** For each bookmark the run moved on a remote, undo shows `bookmark@origin N → O` and asks, then pushes it back with the lease set to N, the commit the run left there. If someone pushed on top of N since, the lease fails and undo reports that, and doesn't force.

**4. Activity after the run.** In the agent-repo, the session's own snapshots always come after the run. Those are expected, and point 2 keeps their content. Anything else after the run, like another vc-x1 command or a raw jj command, makes undo refuse and name what happened. Otherwise undoing "the last run" would also silently undo that later work.

**5. One level for now.** Undoing the last run only. Multi-level undo and redo can come later, and the op tags already support both.

## The ladder

1. **the opening**, retitled to something like **feat: undo takes back the last vc-x1 run**. The cycle title isn't fixed yet.
2. **each write records its run**: op tags on every vc-x1 write, in both repos
3. **undo restores the repos**: `undo -s w|a|b|p`, commits and bookmarks to before the run, the working copy keeping what's on disk, later activity refused
4. **undo rolls back the run's pushes**: asking first, lease set to N
5. **docs and agent-files**: undo is how to recover, with no `jj op restore` needed
6. **the closing**

The acceptance check is your scenario as a test:
- hours of work in the work `@`, then `squash-push -s b`
- `undo -s b` brings the work back into `@`, puts `@-` back as it was, and returns the remote bookmark to O
- the agent journal written in between survives

The order after this: the reshaped push and squash rules ("show what you take", force-with-lease, squash's `--yes` retired), then `squash --include`.

The plain version: build undo first, as its own multi-step cycle. Each vc-x1 command leaves a marker in jj's own history so undo knows exactly what to take back. Undo restores the commits but never the files on disk, so neither your edits nor the running session's transcript get clobbered. And it asks before pushing anything back to the remote.

### feat: undo takes back the last vc-x1 run

Picked from `## Todo` as **undo takes back the last operation** (wink + agent, 2026-10-28), at the
opening of **push refuses rewriting the work trunk**, which this opening first carried and gave up
for this, wink's call (2026-10-28): undo is the safety net the push and squash rules lean on, so it
comes first. Run in the v0.3.1 form, wink's call (2026-10-28): every cycle from now on.

#### Problem

A vc-x1 write is local and so can be taken back, but only by raw jj, `jj op restore` in each repo,
two op logs for `-s b`, the agent-repo's moving with every session write. A `squash-push -s b` that
folds hours of uncommitted work into `@-` by mistake and pushes it leaves the work recoverable from
the op log and the remote rewritten, and getting both back means finding the right operation in each
repo by hand, restoring without clobbering the files on disk, and pushing the bookmark back past a
lease that the restore has made stale.

#### Solution

- Each vc-x1 write records its run: every transaction a run makes carries the run's id and command
  as operation attributes, `Transaction::set_attribute` set in `Session::start_tx`, so the op log
  itself says which operations were vc-x1's, with no state file to disagree with it.
- `undo -s w|a|b|p` takes back the last run in the scoped repos, `-s b` both together:
  - the commits and bookmarks are restored to the operation before the run's first
  - the working copy keeps what is on disk now, `@` made to hold it, so an edit after the run and
    the agent journal the session keeps appending to are never cut back
  - an operation after the run other than a working-copy snapshot, another vc-x1 run or a raw jj
    command, is refused and named, since undoing the run would undo it too.
- undo rolls back what the run pushed: each remote bookmark the run moved, from O to N, is shown and
  asked for, then pushed back to O with the lease at N, so a remote someone moved since is reported
  rather than overwritten.
- One level: the last run. Several levels and a redo are later, the attributes carrying them.
- The help, the README, and the agent-files name undo as how a mistake is taken back.

#### Acceptance check

`cargo test` passes with tests that:

- every write command's operations carry the run's attributes, in each repo it touches
- the mistake: hours of work in the work `@`, `squash-push -s b`, then `undo -s b` puts the work back
  in `@`, `@-` as it was, and the work bookmark on `origin` back at O, and an agent journal written
  in between survives
- `undo -s w`, `-s a`, and `-s p` take back their own repo's run alone
- an operation after the run is refused and named, a declined push-back leaves the remote as it is,
  and a remote moved since the run fails its lease and is reported.

- Undo first, wink's call (2026-10-28): the rules that stop refusing rewrites rest on everything
  local being undoable, so the net is built before the rules change. The push material went back
  to `## Todo` as **squash-push shows what it takes, and push follows jj**.

  mistake and pushing it. jj keeps every earlier state, so nothing is lost locally, and the push is
  the part with no one-command way back.
- The op log is the record, not a file: the attributes travel with the operations, so the last run
  is found by reading the log, and what it pushed by comparing the remote-tracking bookmarks before
  and after it.
- The files on disk are not restored: a plain `jj op restore` checks out the old `@`, which would cut
  the live session's journal back and overwrite edits made since.
- The push-back asks: it is an outward action, so it takes the user's go like any push.
- Multi-step: the recording, the local restore, the push-back, and the docs, each reviewable alone.

### feat: undo takes back the last vc-x1 run

Picked from `## Todo` as **undo takes back the last operation** (wink + agent, 2026-10-28), at the
opening of **push refuses rewriting the work trunk**, which this opening first carried and gave up
for this, wink's call (2026-10-28): undo is the safety net the push and squash rules lean on, so it
comes first. Run in the v0.3.1 form, wink's call (2026-10-28): every cycle from now on.

#### Problem

A vc-x1 write is local and so can be taken back, but only by raw jj, `jj op restore` in each repo,
two op logs for `-s b`, the agent-repo's moving with every session write. A `squash-push -s b` that
folds hours of uncommitted work into `@-` by mistake and pushes it leaves the work recoverable from
the op log and the remote rewritten, and getting both back means finding the right operation in each
repo by hand, restoring without clobbering the files on disk, and pushing the bookmark back past a
lease that the restore has made stale.

#### Solution

- Each vc-x1 write records its run: every transaction a run makes carries the run's id and command
  as operation attributes, `Transaction::set_attribute` set in `Session::start_tx`, so the op log
  itself says which operations were vc-x1's, with no state file to disagree with it.
- `undo -s w|a|b|p` takes back the last run in the scoped repos, `-s b` both together:
  - the commits and bookmarks are restored to the operation before the run's first
  - the working copy keeps what is on disk now, `@` made to hold it, so an edit after the run and
    the agent journal the session keeps appending to are never cut back
  - an operation after the run other than a working-copy snapshot, another vc-x1 run or a raw jj
    command, is refused and named, since undoing the run would undo it too.
- undo rolls back what the run pushed: each remote bookmark the run moved, from O to N, is shown and
  asked for, then pushed back to O with the lease at N, so a remote someone moved since is reported
  rather than overwritten.
- One level: the last run. Several levels and a redo are later, the attributes carrying them.
- The help, the README, and the agent-files name undo as how a mistake is taken back.

#### Acceptance check

`cargo test` passes with tests that:

- every write command's operations carry the run's attributes, in each repo it touches
- the mistake: hours of work in the work `@`, `squash-push -s b`, then `undo -s b` puts the work back
  in `@`, `@-` as it was, and the work bookmark on `origin` back at O, and an agent journal written
  in between survives
- `undo -s w`, `-s a`, and `-s p` take back their own repo's run alone
- an operation after the run is refused and named, a declined push-back leaves the remote as it is,
  and a remote moved since the run fails its lease and is reported.

#### Deliberation

- Undo first, wink's call (2026-10-28): the rules that stop refusing rewrites rest on everything
  local being undoable, so the net is built before the rules change. The push material went back
  to `## Todo` as **squash-push shows what it takes, and push follows jj**.
- The scenario that decided it, wink's (2026-10-28): a `squash-push -s b` folding hours of work by
  mistake and pushing it. jj keeps every earlier state, so nothing is lost locally, and the push is
  the part with no one-command way back.
- The op log is the record, not a file: the attributes travel with the operations, so the last run
  is found by reading the log, and what it pushed by comparing the remote-tracking bookmarks before
  and after it.
- The files on disk are not restored: a plain `jj op restore` checks out the old `@`, which would cut
  the live session's journal back and overwrite edits made since.
- The push-back asks: it is an outward action, so it takes the user's go like any push.
- Multi-step: the recording, the local restore, the push-back, and the docs, each reviewable alone.

### feat: undo takes back the last vc-x1 run

Picked from `## Todo` as **undo takes back the last operation** (wink + agent, 2026-10-28), at the
opening of **push refuses rewriting the work trunk**, which this opening first carried and gave up
for this, wink's call (2026-10-28): undo is the safety net the push and squash rules lean on, so it
comes first. Run in the v0.3.1 form, wink's call (2026-10-28): every cycle from now on.

#### Problem

A vc-x1 write is local and so can be taken back, but only by raw jj, `jj op restore` in each repo,
two op logs for `-s b`, the agent-repo's moving with every session write. A `squash-push -s b` that
folds hours of uncommitted work into `@-` by mistake and pushes it leaves the work recoverable from
the op log and the remote rewritten, and getting both back means finding the right operation in each
repo by hand, restoring without clobbering the files on disk, and pushing the bookmark back past a
lease that the restore has made stale.

#### Solution

- Each vc-x1 write records its run: every transaction a run makes carries the run's id and command
  as operation attributes, `Transaction::set_attribute` set in `Session::start_tx`, so the op log
  itself says which operations were vc-x1's, with no state file to disagree with it.
- `undo -s w|a|b|p` takes back the last run in the scoped repos, `-s b` both together:
  - the commits and bookmarks are restored to the operation before the run's first
  - the working copy keeps what is on disk now, `@` made to hold it, so an edit after the run and
    the agent journal the session keeps appending to are never cut back
  - an operation after the run other than a working-copy snapshot, another vc-x1 run or a raw jj
    command, is refused and named, since undoing the run would undo it too.
- undo rolls back what the run pushed: each remote bookmark the run moved, from O to N, is shown and
  asked for, then pushed back to O with the lease at N, so a remote someone moved since is reported
  rather than overwritten.
- One level: the last run. Several levels and a redo are later, the attributes carrying them.
- The help, the README, and the agent-files name undo as how a mistake is taken back.

#### Acceptance check

`cargo test` passes with tests that:

- every write command's operations carry the run's attributes, in each repo it touches
- the mistake: hours of work in the work `@`, `squash-push -s b`, then `undo -s b` puts the work back
  in `@`, `@-` as it was, and the work bookmark on `origin` back at O, and an agent journal written
  in between survives
- `undo -s w`, `-s a`, and `-s p` take back their own repo's run alone
- an operation after the run is refused and named, a declined push-back leaves the remote as it is,
  and a remote moved since the run fails its lease and is reported.

#### Deliberation

- Undo first, wink's call (2026-10-28): the rules that stop refusing rewrites rest on everything
  local being undoable, so the net is built before the rules change. The push material went back
  to `## Todo` as **squash-push shows what it takes, and push follows jj**.
- The scenario that decided it, wink's (2026-10-28): a `squash-push -s b` folding hours of work by
  mistake and pushing it. jj keeps every earlier state, so nothing is lost locally, and the push is
  the part with no one-command way back.
- The op log is the record, not a file: the attributes travel with the operations, so the last run
  is found by reading the log, and what it pushed by comparing the remote-tracking bookmarks before
  and after it.
- The files on disk are not restored: a plain `jj op restore` checks out the old `@`, which would cut
  the live session's journal back and overwrite edits made since.
- The push-back asks: it is an outward action, so it takes the user's go like any push.
- Multi-step: the recording, the local restore, the push-back, and the docs, each reviewable alone.

record's home, and the cycle that makes this file the rule is [The cycle-record moves out of
TODO.md into zDOING.md](TODO.md#the-cycle-record-moves-out-of-todomd-into-zdoingmd).

## Continuation notes

Where the agent was, for the agent that comes next. Ephemeral, never a record: read first, acted

where [Acquaint](AGENTS.md#acquaint) still says to look.

## In Progress

### feat: undo takes back the last vc-x1 run

Picked from `## Todo` as **undo takes back the last operation** (wink + agent, 2026-10-28), at the
opening of **push refuses rewriting the work trunk**, which this opening first carried and gave up
for this, wink's call (2026-10-28): undo is the safety net the push and squash rules lean on, so it
comes first. Run in the v0.3.1 form, wink's call (2026-10-28): every cycle from now on.

#### Problem

A vc-x1 write is local and so can be taken back, but only by raw jj, `jj op restore` in each repo,
two op logs for `-s b`, the agent-repo's moving with every session write. A `squash-push -s b` that
folds hours of uncommitted work into `@-` by mistake and pushes it leaves the work recoverable from
the op log and the remote rewritten, and getting both back means finding the right operation in each
repo by hand, restoring without clobbering the files on disk, and pushing the bookmark back past a
lease that the restore has made stale.

#### Solution

- Each vc-x1 write records its run: every transaction a run makes carries the run's id and command
  as operation attributes, `Transaction::set_attribute` set in `Session::start_tx`, so the op log
  itself says which operations were vc-x1's, with no state file to disagree with it.
- `undo -s w|a|b|p` takes back the last run in the scoped repos, `-s b` both together:
  - the commits and bookmarks are restored to the operation before the run's first
  - the working copy keeps what is on disk now, `@` made to hold it, so an edit after the run and
    the agent journal the session keeps appending to are never cut back
  - an operation after the run other than a working-copy snapshot, another vc-x1 run or a raw jj
    command, is refused and named, since undoing the run would undo it too.
- undo rolls back what the run pushed: each remote bookmark the run moved, from O to N, is shown and
  asked for, then pushed back to O with the lease at N, so a remote someone moved since is reported
  rather than overwritten.
- One level: the last run. Several levels and a redo are later, the attributes carrying them.
- The help, the README, and the agent-files name undo as how a mistake is taken back.

#### Acceptance check

`cargo test` passes with tests that:

- every write command's operations carry the run's attributes, in each repo it touches
- the mistake: hours of work in the work `@`, `squash-push -s b`, then `undo -s b` puts the work back
  in `@`, `@-` as it was, and the work bookmark on `origin` back at O, and an agent journal written
  in between survives
- `undo -s w`, `-s a`, and `-s p` take back their own repo's run alone
- an operation after the run is refused and named, a declined push-back leaves the remote as it is,
  and a remote moved since the run fails its lease and is reported.

#### Deliberation

- Undo first, wink's call (2026-10-28): the rules that stop refusing rewrites rest on everything
  local being undoable, so the net is built before the rules change. The push material went back
  to `## Todo` as **squash-push shows what it takes, and push follows jj**.
- The scenario that decided it, wink's (2026-10-28): a `squash-push -s b` folding hours of work by
  mistake and pushing it. jj keeps every earlier state, so nothing is lost locally, and the push is
  the part with no one-command way back.
- The op log is the record, not a file: the attributes travel with the operations, so the last run
  is found by reading the log, and what it pushed by comparing the remote-tracking bookmarks before
  and after it.
- The files on disk are not restored: a plain `jj op restore` checks out the old `@`, which would cut
  the live session's journal back and overwrite edits made since.
- The push-back asks: it is an outward action, so it takes the user's go like any push.
- Multi-step: the recording, the local restore, the push-back, and the docs, each reviewable alone.

## Continuation notes

Where the agent was, for the agent that comes next. Ephemeral, never a record: read first, acted
on, and reset to `_None._` by the reader. Kept here by the trial and no longer in `TODO.md`,
where [Acquaint](AGENTS.md#acquaint) still says to look.

_None._

## In Progress

### feat: undo takes back the last vc-x1 run

Picked from `## Todo` as **undo takes back the last operation** (wink + agent, 2026-10-28), at the
opening of **push refuses rewriting the work trunk**, which this opening first carried and gave up
for this, wink's call (2026-10-28): undo is the safety net the push and squash rules lean on, so it
comes first. Run in the v0.3.1 form, wink's call (2026-10-28): every cycle from now on.

#### Problem

A vc-x1 write is local and so can be taken back, but only by raw jj, `jj op restore` in each repo,
two op logs for `-s b`, the agent-repo's moving with every session write. A `squash-push -s b` that
folds hours of uncommitted work into `@-` by mistake and pushes it leaves the work recoverable from
the op log and the remote rewritten, and getting both back means finding the right operation in each
repo by hand, restoring without clobbering the files on disk, and pushing the bookmark back past a
lease that the restore has made stale.

#### Solution

- Each vc-x1 write records its run: every transaction a run makes carries the run's id and command
  as operation attributes, `Transaction::set_attribute` set in `Session::start_tx`, so the op log
  itself says which operations were vc-x1's, with no state file to disagree with it.
- `undo -s w|a|b|p` takes back the last run in the scoped repos, `-s b` both together:
  - the commits and bookmarks are restored to the operation before the run's first
  - the working copy keeps what is on disk now, `@` made to hold it, so an edit after the run and
    the agent journal the session keeps appending to are never cut back
  - an operation after the run other than a working-copy snapshot, another vc-x1 run or a raw jj
    command, is refused and named, since undoing the run would undo it too.
- undo rolls back what the run pushed: each remote bookmark the run moved, from O to N, is shown and
  asked for, then pushed back to O with the lease at N, so a remote someone moved since is reported
  rather than overwritten.
- One level: the last run. Several levels and a redo are later, the attributes carrying them.
- The help, the README, and the agent-files name undo as how a mistake is taken back.

#### Acceptance check

`cargo test` passes with tests that:

- every write command's operations carry the run's attributes, in each repo it touches
- the mistake: hours of work in the work `@`, `squash-push -s b`, then `undo -s b` puts the work back
  in `@`, `@-` as it was, and the work bookmark on `origin` back at O, and an agent journal written
  in between survives
- `undo -s w`, `-s a`, and `-s p` take back their own repo's run alone
- an operation after the run is refused and named, a declined push-back leaves the remote as it is,
  and a remote moved since the run fails its lease and is reported.

#### Deliberation

- Undo first, wink's call (2026-10-28): the rules that stop refusing rewrites rest on everything
  local being undoable, so the net is built before the rules change. The push material went back
  to `## Todo` as **squash-push shows what it takes, and push follows jj**.
- The scenario that decided it, wink's (2026-10-28): a `squash-push -s b` folding hours of work by
  mistake and pushing it. jj keeps every earlier state, so nothing is lost locally, and the push is
  the part with no one-command way back.
- The op log is the record, not a file: the attributes travel with the operations, so the last run
  is found by reading the log, and what it pushed by comparing the remote-tracking bookmarks before
  and after it.
- The files on disk are not restored: a plain `jj op restore` checks out the old `@`, which would cut
  the live session's journal back and overwrite edits made since.
- The push-back asks: it is an outward action, so it takes the user's go like any push.
- **sync --undo takes back the last sync** may become a case of it, a sync being a vc-x1 run.
- Multi-step: the recording, the local restore, the push-back, and the docs, each reviewable alone.

### feat: undo takes back the last vc-x1 run

Picked from `## Todo` as **undo takes back the last operation** (wink + agent, 2026-10-28), at the
opening of **push refuses rewriting the work trunk**, which this opening first carried and gave up
for this, wink's call (2026-10-28): undo is the safety net the push and squash rules lean on, so it
comes first. Run in the v0.3.1 form, wink's call (2026-10-28): every cycle from now on.

#### Problem

A vc-x1 write is local and so can be taken back, but only by raw jj, `jj op restore` in each repo,
two op logs for `-s b`, the agent-repo's moving with every session write. A `squash-push -s b` that
folds hours of uncommitted work into `@-` by mistake and pushes it leaves the work recoverable from
the op log and the remote rewritten, and getting both back means finding the right operation in each
repo by hand, restoring without clobbering the files on disk, and pushing the bookmark back past a
lease that the restore has made stale.

#### Solution

- Each vc-x1 write records its run: every transaction a run makes carries the run's id and command
  as operation attributes, `Transaction::set_attribute` set in `Session::start_tx`, so the op log
  itself says which operations were vc-x1's, with no state file to disagree with it.
- `undo -s w|a|b|p` takes back the last run in the scoped repos, `-s b` both together:
  - the commits and bookmarks are restored to the operation before the run's first
  - the working copy keeps what is on disk now, `@` made to hold it, so an edit after the run and
    the agent journal the session keeps appending to are never cut back
  - an operation after the run other than a working-copy snapshot, another vc-x1 run or a raw jj
    command, is refused and named, since undoing the run would undo it too.
- undo rolls back what the run pushed: each remote bookmark the run moved, from O to N, is shown and
  asked for, then pushed back to O with the lease at N, so a remote someone moved since is reported
  rather than overwritten.
- One level: the last run. Several levels and a redo are later, the attributes carrying them.
- The help, the README, and the agent-files name undo as how a mistake is taken back.

#### Acceptance check

`cargo test` passes with tests that:

- every write command's operations carry the run's attributes, in each repo it touches
- the mistake: hours of work in the work `@`, `squash-push -s b`, then `undo -s b` puts the work back
  in `@`, `@-` as it was, and the work bookmark on `origin` back at O, and an agent journal written
  in between survives
- `undo -s w`, `-s a`, and `-s p` take back their own repo's run alone
- an operation after the run is refused and named, a declined push-back leaves the remote as it is,
  and a remote moved since the run fails its lease and is reported.

#### Deliberation

- Undo first, wink's call (2026-10-28): the rules that stop refusing rewrites rest on everything
  local being undoable, so the net is built before the rules change. The push material went back
  to `## Todo` as **squash-push shows what it takes, and push follows jj**.
- The scenario that decided it, wink's (2026-10-28): a `squash-push -s b` folding hours of work by
  mistake and pushing it. jj keeps every earlier state, so nothing is lost locally, and the push is
  the part with no one-command way back.
- The op log is the record, not a file: the attributes travel with the operations, so the last run
  is found by reading the log, and what it pushed by comparing the remote-tracking bookmarks before
  and after it.
- The files on disk are not restored: a plain `jj op restore` checks out the old `@`, which would cut
  the live session's journal back and overwrite edits made since.
- The push-back asks: it is an outward action, so it takes the user's go like any push.
- Multi-step: the recording, the local restore, the push-back, and the docs, each reviewable alone.

#### Ladder

- [feat: undo takes back the last vc-x1 run opening][p0] (current)
- [feat: each vc-x1 write records its run in the op log][p1]
- [feat: undo restores the repos to before the last run][p2]
- [feat: undo rolls back the last run's pushes][p3]
- [docs: undo is how a mistake is taken back][p4]
- [feat: undo takes back the last vc-x1 run closing][p5]

[package]
name = "vc-x1"
version = "0.85.16-0"
edition = "2024"

# The package name is the installed binary's name and never
# changes: a cycle's validation installs under its own root,
# `--root tmp/dev` in `.vc-config.md`'s `[validate]` lists, so a
# dev build (a suffixed version) never replaces the stable
# `vc-x1` on the PATH. The promotion is the plain `cargo install`
# from `main`. Before 2026-10-20 a cycle renamed the package to
# `vc-x1-dev` instead, guarded by build.rs (chores-16, 0.78.3).

[lints.clippy]
# The process-spawn ban: `Command::new` is disallowed via
# clippy.toml's `disallowed-methods`, and deny (not warn) so a bare
# new spawn site fails `cargo clippy` even without `-D warnings`.
# The documented allowlist lives in clippy.toml.
disallowed_methods = "deny"

[dependencies]
chrono = { version = "0.4", default-features = false, features = ["now"] }
clap = { version = "4.6", features = ["derive", "wrap_help"] }
clap_complete = { version = "4.6", features = ["unstable-dynamic"] }
futures = "0.3"
# The gix jj-lib 0.46 resolves (no features of our own): the
# session's lock-contention downcast needs type identity with the
# errors jj-lib returns, and init's bare-repo creation reuses it.
gix = { version = "0.88", default-features = false }
# When raising jj-lib: check whether it now offers the commits a
# remote's bookmarks are on without fetching. If so, `git_command`
# in src/jj/session.rs and its two callers take it, and
# clippy.toml's register entry 6 closes (TODO.md > ## Waiting).
jj-lib = "0.46"
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["std"] }
pollster = "1.0"
# The rng jj-lib's `SecureConfig` takes to mint a repo's config id,
# at jj-lib 0.46's versions so the types are its own, seeded the way
# jj-cli seeds it (src/jj/session.rs `load_repo_config`).
rand = "0.10"
rand_chacha = "0.10"
serde_json = "1"

[target.'cfg(unix)'.dependencies]
libc = "0.2"

- anthropic-skills:import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- anthropic-skills:morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.
</system-reminder>
